chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Said from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from Al-Halabi from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): In

the mukatab (slave who has contracted for manumission for a specified sum) who pays part of his manumission money, he said: 'Indeed, the people used not to stipulate [a condition of return if unable to pay], but today they do stipulate. And Muslims are upon their conditions. So if he stipulated upon him that if he became unable [to pay], he would return [to slavery], and if he did not stipulate upon him, he would not return.'
And regarding the saying of Allah, Exalted and Mighty: 'So write for them if you know in them any good' (1), he said: 'Write for them if you know they have wealth.'

key_terms.إِنْ عَجَزَ: If he became unable: Referring to the inability to pay the remaining balance.
key_terms.اَلْمُكَاتَبِ: Mukatab: A slave who has entered into a contract with his master to buy his freedom for a specified sum.
key_terms.خَيْراً: Good: In this context, referring to financial capability or wealth.
key_terms.رَجَعَ: He returned: Referring to returning to slavery.
key_terms.عِنْدَ شُرُوطِهِمْ: Upon their conditions: A legal principle meaning the validity of conditions in contracts is respected.
key_terms.يَشْتَرِطُونَ: They stipulate: To include specific conditions in a contract.

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if a mukatab cannot pay the rest of his manumission price?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the contractual rights of a *mukatab* (slave seeking manumission), establishing that the master's right to reclaim the slave upon payment default exists only if explicitly stipulated, reflecting the Shia legal principle that 'Muslims are bound by their conditions' (*al-muslimun 'ala shurutihim*). It further interprets the Quranic phrase 'if you know in them any good' as specifically referring to financial solvency, a nuance highlighted by scholars like Al-Tusi to distinguish general merit from economic capability in manumission contracts.
